translations.note: Os sacrum, 'the sacred bone', is the anatomical name for the sacrum, the triangular bone at the base of the spine.
The thin inner membrane that lies directly on the brain.
The tough outer membrane of the brain.

The standard anatomical name, still used in English, for the innermost membrane covering the brain. It is kept as a term here, as Burton uses it. Literally it means 'tender (or pious) mother', a medieval Latin rendering of an Arabic anatomical name. Burton's English after it describes the membrane but does not translate the name.
Pituita is phlegm, one of the four humours. Older anatomy held that the brain's ventricles drained it away.
Greek mēninx, 'membrane', used particularly of the membranes of the brain.
Greek-derived anatomical term, 'the region over the stomach', meaning the upper abdomen. Burton's following 'upper and lower' glosses this pair of terms.
Greek-derived anatomical term, 'the region under the stomach', meaning the lower abdomen. Burton glosses it with 'lower' in his 'upper and lower'.
The upper abdomen. Mirach, which follows, is the Arabic name for it as used in Latin translations of the Arabic physicians.
The fatty fold of membrane that hangs from the stomach. Burton glosses it as 'Kell or Caul'.

translations.text: and only the chief and larger ones at that: for the rest, let whoever wishes take it from the books On the Soul

translations.note: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Burton glosses it as 'Rim of the belly'.
The name comes from duodeni, 'twelve each', after its length of about twelve finger-breadths. Burton's 'some twelve inches long' alludes to this. He calls it the 'whole gut'.
The membrane that holds the intestines in place. Burton's gloss 'Midriff' is loose, since the midriff is properly the diaphragm.
A Greek anatomical term used in Latin, meaning a partition. Burton gives the English 'Midriff' just before it.
Chyle: the milky fluid that early physiology said the stomach made from food in the 'first concoction'.
From the Greek pylōros, 'gatekeeper': the lower opening of the stomach. Burton's 'nether door' describes it, but it is not a translation of the name.

translations.note: Short for arteria venosa, the 'venous artery': the vessel now called the pulmonary vein. Burton calls it 'the Venosal Artery' further on.

A term from canon law. A legatus a latere was a papal legate sent 'from the Pope's side': a cardinal of the highest rank with full delegated powers. In Burton's image the liver is the full deputy of the heart, which he calls the king.

burton_span.exact: admiration, that can yield such variety of affections

1.1.2.4-f5.text: Haec res est praecipue digna admiratione, quod tanta affectuum varietate cietur cor, quod omnes res tristes & laetae statim corda feriunt & movent

translations.literal: This thing is especially worthy of admiration, that by so great a variety of affections the heart is stirred, that all things sad and glad immediately strike and move hearts.
translations.note: Burton's main text, at the point where this note is anchored, renders the first half loosely ('a part worthy of admiration, that can yield such variety of affections'). The second clause, about sad and joyful things striking the heart at once, has no counterpart in his English. The plural 'corda' (hearts) is rendered as a singular for natural English.

burton_span.exact: admiration, that can yield such variety of affections

translations.text: This is especially worthy of admiration: that the heart is stirred by so great a variety of affections, and that all things, sad and joyful alike, at once strike and move the heart.

translations.note: Melancholy arising from the mirach (the epigastric region): the Arabic physicians' name for what is elsewhere called hypochondriacal melancholy.
The great vein that returns blood to the right side of the heart.
Aspera arteria, 'the rough artery', is the old name for the trachea, so called from its rings of cartilage. The ancients thought it carried air like an artery.
The tough outer membrane of the brain. The name, 'hard mother', goes back to a medieval rendering of Arabic terms.
